title: Does Religion Cause War?
objective: After this level you can weigh the explanations scholars give for conflicts called religious, separating faith from land, power and identity.
summary: Juergensmeyer shows how religion frames conflict as 'cosmic war' but not as its root cause; Cavanaugh calls 'religious violence' a misleading category.

cards.headline: Does religion cause war? Two leading scholars give different answers.
cards.body: Mark Juergensmeyer studies what religion adds to violence. William Cavanaugh asks whether "religious violence" is even a useful category. Weigh them together, and a better question appears.

cards.headline: Juergensmeyer: a war in the heavens
cards.body: In Terror in the Mind of God, Juergensmeyer studied violence in Christian, Muslim, Jewish, Hindu, Sikh and Buddhist groups, drawing on interviews. His key idea is "cosmic war": not just a fight for religious reasons, but the image of a broader conflict between good and evil, right and wrong. Seen this way, an earthly struggle feels like a battle with eternity at stake.

cards.headline: But not the root cause
cards.body: So is religion the cause? "I don't believe that for a moment," Juergensmeyer said. Violence, in his view, happens for a complex variety of social, political and economic reasons. What religious images and language bring is "a structure of justification and meaning".

cards.headline: Cavanaugh: a slippery category
cards.body: Cavanaugh goes further. In The Myth of Religious Violence (2009) he argues there is no timeless, cross-cultural essence of religion: what counts as religious or secular depends on who holds power. So the idea that religion is uniquely irrational and violent is, he argues, one of the founding myths of Western society.

cards.headline: Separate the threads
cards.body: Put side by side, the two overlap more than they clash. Neither treats faith as the whole story: Juergensmeyer points to social, political and economic causes, and Cavanaugh to power. So when a conflict is called religious, ask what else is at stake, like land, power or identity. Then ask what the religious language adds.

mascot.line: Watch the word: Cavanaugh's 'myth' is the everyday kind, a belief he thinks is mistaken, not Level 4's sacred story.

cards.headline: Does Religion Cause War?: the takeaways
learned: Juergensmeyer: religion frames conflict as cosmic war
Violence has social, political and economic causes too
Cavanaugh: 'religious violence' is a slippery category

questions.prompt: What does Juergensmeyer call the image of a conflict as a broader struggle between good and evil?

options.label: Holy war
options.rationale: He chose a different term to mean more than a fight for religious reasons.

options.label: Just war
options.rationale: That's an idea from ethics, not his term.

questions.explanation: 'Cosmic war' is his name for picturing a conflict as good against evil, right against wrong.

questions.prompt: Which claim belongs to Cavanaugh's argument rather than Juergensmeyer's?

options.label: Religious images give violence a structure of meaning
Religion alone is the main cause of most wars
What counts as 'religious' depends on who holds power
Violence studied across six traditions, through interviews

questions.explanation: Cavanaugh argues there's no timeless essence of religion, so drawing the religious and secular line is itself shaped by power.

questions.prompt: Cavanaugh says religion has no timeless, cross-cultural essence. Which Level 2 finding supports his starting point?

options.label: Rites of passage appear in all known societies
options.rationale: That points to something universal, not the reverse.

options.label: Göbekli Tepe was built before farming
The concept of religion reached East Asia only about a century ago
Christianity is the world's largest religion
options.rationale: Size says nothing about the category.

questions.explanation: If the very concept of religion arrived in East Asia recently, and fits its traditions awkwardly, the category isn't timeless.
